title: CMOS inverter amplifier
description: A CMOS inverter used as an analog amplifier: the input drives both an NMOS and a PMOS gate, and the two devices share one drain current stacked between the rails (current reuse). Because both transconductances act on the same input, the stage transconductance is the sum $g_{m,tot} = g_{m,n} + g_{m,p}$, so the inverter gives roughly twice the $g_m$ of a single device at the same current - the reason it is the workhorse gain cell for low-voltage, power-efficient design. The gain is $g_{m,tot}/(g_{ds,n} + g_{ds,p})$. Both devices are composed children biased at the same current; pick the PMOS child table to the p polarity and set p_sign to -1 for a signed-PMOS axis. The input DC level $V_{in}$ is a spec you state, and each device's sizing then implies its own value for that same node: the NMOS gate sits one $V_{GS}$ above ground, the PMOS gate one $V_{GS}$ below the supply. Two consistency guardrails compare $V_{in}$ against both, because one shared gate carrying one shared current leaves a single real degree of freedom between the two inversion levels — satisfying both at once requires $V_{GS,n} + |V_{GS,p}| = V_{DD}$, a constraint on the pair rather than a choice made twice. Reconciling them is the design work this sheet exists to show.

params.name: V_out
params.note: output DC level; sets both devices' drain-source voltages (ideally near mid-supply)

params.name: V_in
params.note: input DC level — the voltage on the shared gate. An inverting amplifier is biased at its own trip point, where the input and output levels coincide, so mid-supply is the usual starting choice. Both devices are checked against this node rather than either one defining it

params.name: cdd_est
params.note: output-node parasitic estimate (both drains + wiring); refine from extraction

params.name: I_bias
params.note: the single current both devices carry (current reuse)

params.name: gm_id_p
params.note: PMOS inversion. Matching it to gm_id_n balances the transfer and minimizes offset, but the two devices share one gate, so this choice also places the input level — see the V_in_p row and the input-consistent-p guardrail

params.name: p_sign
params.note: vds sign convention of the PMOS table: +1 for an N-style axis, -1 for a signed-PMOS axis

doc.title: NMOS device
doc.description: The pull-down device at the shared current, drain at the output. Exposes its transconductance, output conductance, saturation headroom, current, gate-source voltage, and channel-noise density. Its wiring declaration puts the shared gate at $V_{in}$ above a grounded source, which this bind must then agree with: the input level is stated, not read off this device, so the check compares two independently chosen numbers.

doc.title: PMOS device
doc.description: The pull-up device at the shared current, drain at the output. Exposes its transconductance, output conductance, saturation headroom, current, and gate-source voltage — the last so the sheet can place the shared gate one gate-source voltage below the supply.

params.name: vds_d
params.note: source-to-drain headroom, signed to this table's axis convention

rows.name: V_in_n
rows.note: where the NMOS sizing puts the shared gate: its source is at ground, so the gate sits at its own gate-source voltage

rows.name: V_in_p
rows.note: where the PMOS sizing puts the same gate: its source is at VDD, so the gate sits one gate-source voltage below the supply. abs() because a signed-PMOS table keeps that axis negative

rows.name: gm_tot
rows.note: current reuse: both devices' transconductances act on the same input and add

rows.name: gout
rows.note: both output conductances load the node

rows.name: Rout
rows.note: the resistance this stage presents at its output — both devices' output conductances in parallel. The gain assumes a capacitive load, so nothing here models a resistive one; this row is what a composing parent checks its own loading against

rows.name: Av
rows.note: combined transconductance into the combined output conductance

rows.name: vn_in
rows.note: both channel-noise currents (each device's own vnth_m*gm) sum and refer to the input by gm_tot

rows.name: cgg_in
rows.note: estimate: the capacitance the input terminal presents. Both gates are driven together, so both gate capacitances load the driver. Gate capacitance only, because the Miller term needs the gate-drain fraction and these tables do not carry it — and here the drain swings against the gate, so that omission is at its worst. No rule reads it

rows.name: I_q
rows.note: estimate: quiescent supply current — the single inverting branch, with both devices stacked on the one current. The datasheet line for comparing designs; no rule reads it

rules.note: NMOS saturated at the output DC level
PMOS saturated: its headroom is the supply minus the output level

the NMOS inversion must put the shared gate where V_in says it is. The tolerance is one percent of the TYPED input level — V_in sits on the right so both sides of the reconciliation are held to the same window in volts, rather than each to a window set by whatever level its own device happened to imply. For any input below one volt that window is tighter than the 10 mV gate-wiring tolerance, so this rule closes first; tune gm_id_n (or L_n, or the bias current) until it does

the same reconciliation on the pull-up side, against the same one percent of the typed input level. The two inversion levels are not independent knobs: one gate carrying one current is a single real degree of freedom, so both rules close together only where V_GS,n + |V_GS,p| equals the supply. Where no pair inside the declared inversion ranges reaches that, the honest answers are a different supply, different lengths, or a different bias current — not a wider range
computed from the gamma-model floor; this table carries no measured noise; the simulator owns noise sign-off
combined gm over the total output capacitance
